title: Containerize a Fastify app
before_you_start: Node.js, npm, Docker, and the starter Fastify app are on the desktop.

role.title: Backend / DevOps engineer
role.company_context: Product-led SaaS company shipping Node services. A small platform team owns local-to-prod container patterns so feature teams can run and ship APIs without reinventing Docker each time. Hiring to strengthen day-to-day containerization and runtime hygiene on that team.
day_to_day: Package and run internal Node/Fastify services in Docker for local and staging use
Keep images lean (multi-stage builds, sensible bases) and document how others rebuild them
Review Dockerfiles and Compose setups for port publishing, health checks, and non-root defaults
Pair with backend engineers on “works on my machine → works in a container” issues
Improve shared templates and conventions for service containerization
required_skills: Comfortable writing Dockerfiles for Node apps (including lockfile-based installs)
Solid grasp of container networking basics (published ports, listen host, health endpoints)
Can explain and apply multi-stage or otherwise lean image practices
Can validate a running container against expected HTTP behavior
nice_to_have_skills: Docker Compose for multi-service or proxy setups
Familiarity with Alpine/slim Node bases and non-root USER patterns
Experience reviewing PRs for container security and image size
Prior work on internal platform or developer-experience tooling
constraints: Assessment focuses on containerizing an existing Fastify app — not redesigning the service or swapping frameworks
Do not test Kubernetes, cloud IaC, or CI pipeline design in this challenge
Candidate works in a desktop environment with Terminal and Docker available
Starter app files in the workspace are shared scenery; do not require inventing a different stack

problem_statement.title: Containerize the Fastify app
problem_statement.summary: A small Node.js (Fastify) service is on your desktop. Your job is to package it so it runs reliably as a container.
outcomes: Build an image that starts the app and serves its HTTP routes.
Expose the service so it can be reached from outside the container on a documented host port.
Keep the runtime image reasonably small and suitable for a production-like baseline (prefer a multi-stage build when dependencies are installed during the image build).
constraints: Do not change the app’s public behavior: GET / and GET /health must keep working as they do today.
The process inside the container should listen on a port you can map (default app port is 3000 unless you document otherwise).
Prefer running the app process as a non-root user in the final image when the base image supports it.
Starter files on the desktop stay as shared scenery — treat them as the application source you containerize; do not replace them with a different stack.
problem_statement.deliverables: Produce whatever files and commands a reviewer needs to rebuild and run your image from this desktop (for example a Dockerfile, and optionally Compose). Leave clear enough structure that someone else can build and start the service without guessing.

rubric.name: Working container
rubric.summary: Demonstrates a running container that serves the app through a published host port.
rubric.description: YES/NO: Did the candidate demonstrate a running container that serves the starter Fastify routes (GET / and/or GET /health) through a published host port mapped to the app’s documented default listen port (see starter index.js / brief)? Answer YES only if video or narrative shows a successful check (browser or curl) against the mapped port. Build-only, crash-on-start, or inferred “probably works” = NO. YES = full points; NO or unclear = 0.

rubric.name: Dockerfile quality
rubric.summary: Uses a lockfile-based install and a lean runtime image in the Dockerfile.
rubric.description: YES/NO: Does the final Dockerfile use a reproducible lockfile install (npm ci or equivalent) and a lean final runtime (multi-stage or alpine/slim Node base, not an unexplained full OS image)? Answer YES only if both are visible in the deliverable Dockerfile. Missing lockfile-based install or a heavyweight unjustified base = NO. YES = full points; NO or unclear = 0.

rubric.name: Runtime hygiene
rubric.summary: Runs the app as a non-root user and documents the container port to publish.
rubric.description: YES/NO: Does the final image configuration run the app as a non-root user (USER or equivalent) and expose/document a container port suitable for publishing (e.g. EXPOSE matching the app default listen port)? Answer YES only if both appear in the final Dockerfile (or equivalent compose). Missing non-root USER or no port exposure/documentation = NO. YES = full points; NO or unclear = 0.

rubric.name: Clarity of deliverables
rubric.summary: Leaves a rebuildable Dockerfile on the desktop that a reviewer can follow without guessing steps.
rubric.description: YES/NO: Is there a Dockerfile (or equivalent) left on the desktop that a reviewer could use to rebuild the image without guessing paths or undocumented steps? Answer YES if the primary build artifact is present and self-explanatory enough to rebuild; optional compose/notes must be accurate if present. No Dockerfile / cannot rebuild from the workspace = NO. YES = full points; NO or unclear = 0.

invariants: Keep the same skills_assessed and rubric structure/weights
Keep the same deliverable kinds and difficulty band (Dockerfile + running container for a small Fastify app)
Keep Fastify, GET / and GET /health public routes, and lockfile-based install expectations
Do not introduce Kubernetes, cloud IaC, or a different application stack
Do not rewrite package-lock.json; keep the same fastify dependency range across instances

values.package_description: Small Fastify hello/health service for containerization practice

apply.candidate_brief:
## Containerize the {{service_label}}

A small Node.js (Fastify) service named `{{package_name}}` is on your desktop. Your job is to package it so it runs reliably as a container.

### Outcomes
- Build an image that starts the app and serves its HTTP routes.
- Expose the service so it can be reached from outside the container on a documented host port.
- Keep the runtime image reasonably small and suitable for a production-like baseline (prefer a multi-stage build when dependencies are installed during the image build).

### Constraints
- Do not change the app’s public behavior: GET / and GET /health must keep working as they do today (including the existing JSON payloads).
- The process inside the container should listen on a port you can map (default app port is {{default_port}} unless you document otherwise).
- Prefer running the app process as a non-root user in the final image when the base image supports it.
- Starter files on the desktop stay as shared scenery — treat them as the application source you containerize; do not replace them with a different stack.

### Deliverables
Produce whatever files and commands a reviewer needs to rebuild and run your image from this desktop (for example a Dockerfile, and optionally Compose). Leave clear enough structure that someone else can build and start the service without guessing.
